script.opening: "Thanks, doctor — honestly I feel a bit silly even booking this. I had a tiny bit of bleeding, you know, down below, just the once when I wiped, and it’s stopped now. It’s probably just dryness or I’ve strained something. I nearly cancelled. Can you just reassure me it’s nothing so I can get on? I don’t want a load of tests at my age."

facts.text: If asked directly: fresh red blood on wiping, postmenopausal (10 years since LMP), 2 days ago, one episode, no trauma, not on HRT, no obvious source she can identify. Even a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding is significant. If asked, a little watery/blood-stained discharge over recent weeks she’d dismissed.

If explored: BMI 33, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, never had children (nulliparous) — a cluster of endometrial cancer risk factors (her menopause at 51 is an average age, not a late one). Mother had "womb trouble" (possibly endometrial/ovarian).

HIDDEN AGENDA — the minimising is fear-driven: she has quietly convinced herself it IS cancer (her mother’s "womb trouble"), and is downplaying it precisely because she is terrified. She booked a VIDEO appointment partly to avoid an examination she dreads. She wants permission to not have it be real.

If reached gently: she is anxious and embarrassed about an internal/speculum examination — a previous unpleasant smear experience years ago — and this is part of why she’s pushing for phone reassurance. Needs this acknowledged, not bulldozed.

Officially: to be reassured it’s nothing and avoid tests/examination. What she needs: clear explanation that postmenopausal bleeding at 55 or over, not attributable to HRT, is a red flag requiring a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12), delivered so she accepts it despite her fear, with the examination dread handled compassionately.

ice.ideas: It was a trivial one-off — dryness or a strain — and almost certainly nothing.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — privately terrified it is womb cancer (her mother’s "womb trouble"), which is exactly why she is minimising it; plus dread of an internal examination after a bad smear experience.
ice.expectations: To be reassured over video and sent away without tests. What she actually needs: urgent NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral for postmenopausal bleeding, accepted despite her fear.

cues: "Probably nothing / I nearly cancelled" — active minimising of a red-flag symptom; the fear is underneath.
Booked a VIDEO appointment and resists examination — the dread of being examined is shaping her behaviour.
"At my age" + a mother with "womb trouble" — the cancer fear she hasn’t voiced.

checkpoints.text: Recognises POSTMENOPAUSAL BLEEDING as a red flag in its own right — even a single episode, 10 years after the LMP, off HRT — and does NOT accept the "dryness/probably nothing" framing or reassure it away

States the NG12 pathway explicitly: unexplained postmenopausal bleeding in a woman aged 55+ that cannot be attributed to HRT (she has never used HRT) is a suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial cancer; the service usually starts with transvaginal ultrasound of the endometrial thickness — restated as the action, tagged NICE NG12; under 55 the referral is "consider"

Identifies the endometrial-cancer risk factors that raise concern further: obesity (BMI 33), type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, hypertension, family history (a family history suggestive of Lynch syndrome is the relevant one to ask about) — and explains (without alarming) why she is someone to take seriously, not reassure

Arranges/encourages examination appropriately: explains an abdominal and pelvic/speculum examination is needed (to look for a local cause — cervix, vagina, atrophy) and that this needs to be in person, handling her dread sensitively rather than skipping it because she booked video

Screens for other relevant features and safety: any heavier/ongoing bleeding, blood-stained discharge, weight loss, and considers cervical screening history (the NHS Cervical Screening Programme invites to age 64); arranges baseline as appropriate without delaying the suspected cancer pathway referral

Hears the fear beneath the minimising and names it gently — does not collude with "it’s nothing", but does not frighten her into disengagement either; explains that urgent referral is precautionary and most PMB is benign (commonly atrophy)
Acknowledges and accommodates the examination dread (the previous bad smear), offering choice, a chaperone, and control, so she accepts the in-person assessment

Safety-nets and follows up: explains the suspected cancer pathway timeframe (appointment within 2 weeks) and what to expect (TVUSS ± biopsy/hysteroscopy), what to do if heavier bleeding/pain occurs meanwhile, ensures she will attend, documents, and arranges to follow up the result — does not leave a frightened patient to navigate it alone

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you didn’t cancel — and I want to be honest with you rather than just reassure you, because you matter too much for that. Any bleeding after the menopause, even a tiny one-off ten years on, is something we always check properly. It’s not silly at all; it’s exactly the kind of thing we want to see."

"There’s a clear national rule for this — the NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, says bleeding after the menopause in a woman your age, when it isn’t down to HRT, needs an urgent referral to the gynaecology team, usually starting with an internal ultrasound scan to look at the lining of the womb. That’s called a suspected cancer pathway referral. It sounds scary, but it’s simply how we make sure we’re not missing anything."

"Let me balance that: most of the time, this kind of bleeding turns out to be something harmless — usually thinning and dryness of the tissues after the menopause. The urgent referral isn’t me telling you it’s cancer; it’s me making absolutely sure it isn’t, quickly. Both those things are true at once."

"Can I gently ask — when you said ‘at my age’, and mentioned your mum’s womb trouble, I wondered if cancer had crossed your mind? … Thank you for telling me. That fear is completely understandable, and it’s the very reason getting this checked fast is the right thing — so you’re not lying awake imagining the worst."

"I do need to examine you in person as well — to look directly for a simple local cause. I know from what you’ve said that examinations have been horrible for you before, and I won’t brush past that. You’re in control: a chaperone, we stop the moment you say, and I’ll talk you through every step. Shall we find a time that works?"

"So: I’m making the urgent referral today, you’ll be contacted within two weeks, and they’ll do the scan and possibly look inside the womb with a tiny camera. If before then you get heavier bleeding or pain, ring us or use the urgent route. I’ll keep an eye out for the result and we’ll go through it together. You came in hoping I’d say it’s nothing — what I’m doing instead is making sure you find out properly and fast."

f.learning: Postmenopausal bleeding is a cardinal red flag and a defined NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway: a woman aged 55 and over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial cancer (under 55: consider it); the service usually starts with transvaginal ultrasound of the endometrial thickness. A single episode, years after the LMP and off HRT, counts — it must never be reassured away as "dryness". This patient stacks endometrial-cancer risk factors (obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, hypertension, family history). The examinable hidden agenda is that her minimising is fear-driven — she suspects cancer (mother’s "womb trouble") and booked a VIDEO appointment partly to dodge an examination she dreads after a bad smear. The skill is to refuse the dismissal without frightening her into disengagement (state the pathway, balance it honestly with the fact most PMB is benign), name and accommodate the examination dread (choice, chaperone, control), and complete the suspected cancer pathway referral with a clear safety-net and follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NHS Cervical Screening Programme · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
knowledge.summary: Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding at 55 or over, not attributable to HRT, is a suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial cancer. One episode is enough.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial cancer if aged 55 and over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT. Under 55: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral. She is 61 and has never used HRT, so she meets the “refer” criterion.
Postmenopausal bleeding is bleeding 12 months or more after the last period. Light, single or self-limiting episodes still need referral; attributing it to dryness without assessment is unsafe.

Obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen and a family history suggestive of Lynch syndrome raise endometrial cancer risk. They add weight to the referral; their absence would not remove it.

Most gynaecology suspected cancer services start with transvaginal ultrasound of the endometrial thickness, then endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy if needed. Explain this so she knows what to expect.

Abdominal and speculum examination looks for a local cause (atrophy, polyp, cervical lesion) and needs a face-to-face appointment. Check her cervical screening history (the programme invites to age 64). Examination should not hold up the referral.
Most postmenopausal bleeding has a benign cause such as atrophy. The referral is how cancer is excluded quickly; it is not a diagnosis. Say both.

Endometrial cancer vs atrophy, polyp, cervical lesion, other bleeding source.
Discharge, weight loss, pain, post-coital bleeding, haematuria and rectal bleeding asked; risk factors identified.
Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding needing exclusion of endometrial cancer, explained honestly.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Recognised obesity, diabetes and nulliparity as risk factors; checked cervical screening status.
What to expect, chase if no contact, heavy bleeding or pain → same day, results reviewed together.

Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Easton, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining the video. Tell me what’s been happening.
I feel silly even booking. A tiny bit of bleeding when I wiped, just once, and it’s stopped. Probably dryness. Can you just reassure me it’s nothing? I don’t want a load of tests at my age.
I’m really glad you didn’t cancel — it isn’t silly at all. I’d like to ask a few questions, then explain what I think and what we should do. Is that alright?
model.why: Validates attending and sets an agenda without colluding

model.text: Alright.
When did your periods stop, and have you ever taken HRT?
model.why: Confirms postmenopausal status and excludes HRT as a cause

model.text: At 51, ten years ago. Never had HRT.
Tell me about the bleeding — colour, amount, and whether there’s been anything else, like discharge, in recent weeks?
model.why: Characterises the bleed and asks about associated discharge

model.text: Fresh red, on the paper, two days ago. Now you mention it, a bit of watery pinkish discharge the last few weeks. I ignored it.
That’s helpful. Any pain, weight loss, bleeding after sex, or blood in your urine or from your back passage?
model.why: Screens for other sources and systemic features

model.text: No, none of that.
Have you had children? And any family history of womb, ovary or bowel cancer?
model.why: Nulliparity and family history as risk factors

model.text: No children. Mum had “womb trouble” — nobody said exactly what.
When did you last have a smear test?
I’d have to check. I had a horrible one years ago and I dread them.
You mentioned your mum, and “at my age”. I wondered whether something more worrying has crossed your mind?
model.why: Picks up the cues and gently surfaces the unspoken fear

model.text: (Quiet.) Cancer. Like Mum. I suppose that’s why I keep saying it’s nothing.
Thank you for telling me. That fear makes complete sense, and it explains why you’ve been hoping I’d say it’s nothing. And the smear — was that part of why you booked a video appointment?
model.why: Validates the fear and names the examination dread

model.text: Yes. I dread being examined.

I want to be honest with you. Any bleeding after the menopause needs checking, even once, ten years on. National guidance says that for a woman over 55 who isn’t on HRT, we refer urgently to the gynaecology team to check the lining of the womb.
model.why: States the NICE NG12 criterion and action

model.text: So you do think it’s cancer.

No. Most bleeding like this turns out to be harmless — often thinning of the tissues after the menopause. The urgent referral isn’t a diagnosis; it’s how we make sure quickly. Some things like weight and diabetes do make checking more important, which is another reason not to wait.
model.why: Balances honesty with reassurance; links risk factors without alarm

model.text: What will they do?
Usually an internal ultrasound scan to measure the womb lining, and sometimes a small sample or a look inside with a thin camera. They’ll explain each step.
model.why: Explains the pathway so she knows what to expect

model.text: I also need to examine you in person, to look for a simple cause like dryness or a polyp. I heard how hard the last one was. You’d be in control: a chaperone, a smaller speculum, and we stop the moment you say. Would that make it manageable?
model.why: Accommodates the examination dread with choice and control

model.text: If I can stop it… yes. I’ll come in.
Thank you. I’ll make the urgent referral today, so the examination won’t hold anything up. We can check your smear history at the same visit.
model.why: Referral not delayed for examination; screening addressed

model.text: Okay.

The hospital should contact you soon — if you haven’t heard within a week, ring us. If you get heavy bleeding, pain or feel unwell before then, contact us the same day. I’ll look out for the result and we’ll go through it together. What will you tell yourself tonight when the worry comes?
model.why: Specific safety-net, tracking of referral, follow-up and teach-back

model.text: That it needs checking quickly, and most of the time it’s nothing bad. And I’m not doing it alone.
That’s exactly right. Anything else before we finish?
No. Thank you for being straight with me.

social.t: Her mother’s “womb trouble” makes cancer feel likely; downplaying it is how she copes. Name it gently.
A bad smear years ago has left her dreading examination. A trauma-informed approach can keep her engaged.

legal.t: She has capacity and can decline referral or examination; if so, explain the risk, document the discussion and keep the door open (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Explain why, offer a chaperone, gain consent, and stop on request (GMC guidance on intimate examinations and chaperones).
Track the suspected cancer referral and make sure she is seen; tell her who will contact her and what to do if they don’t.

community.t: The Eve Appeal (gynaecological cancer charity) has information on postmenopausal bleeding and what tests involve.

redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding at 55 or over, not attributable to HRT: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Blood-stained or watery discharge, weight loss, pelvic pain
Risk factors: obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, family history
psychosocial: Mother’s “womb trouble” and fear of the same
Dread of examination after a bad smear
Living with diabetes and weight — without blame
ice: Concern: cancer, like her mother; being examined
Expectation: reassurance by video and no tests

playbook.diagnosis: “Bleeding after the menopause always needs checking. Most causes are harmless, but the way we make sure is an urgent referral to look at the lining of the womb.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a smoke alarm going off once. Usually it’s burnt toast, but you still check the house — quickly and properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hoping I’d say it’s nothing because of what happened to your mum. I’d rather find out properly and fast, so you’re not lying awake guessing.”
management.psychosocial: Accommodate the examination dread with a chaperone, choice of speculum, and her control to stop.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial cancer today (NICE NG12)
Face-to-face abdominal and speculum examination with chaperone, not delaying the referral
Check cervical screening history and offer screening if due
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, pain or feeling unwell → same-day contact
Ring if no hospital contact within a week; results reviewed together

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you hold a red flag against a patient who wants you to let it go. It is failed by collusion, by frightening her out of the pathway, or by skipping the examination.

items.fail: Accepting “probably dryness” and suggesting vaginal oestrogen or review if it recurs.
items.why: PMB at 61 off HRT meets the NICE NG12 referral criterion. A single episode counts.
items.fix: “Any bleeding after the menopause gets checked — I’m referring you urgently today.”

items.fail: Delaying the referral until after an examination or blood tests.
items.why: Examination matters, but the referral should not wait for it.
items.fix: Refer today and book the in-person examination alongside.

items.fail: Missing the cancer fear under “it’s nothing”.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s concerns.” Her minimising is fear, and unaddressed fear risks non-attendance.
items.fix: “You mentioned your mum — I wondered if cancer had crossed your mind?”

items.fail: Brushing past her dread of examination.
items.why: She booked video to avoid it. Without choice and control, she may not attend.
items.fix: Chaperone, smaller speculum, stop on request, talk her through each step.

items.fail: “We need to rule out cancer” with no context of how often it is benign.
items.fix: Say both truths: most PMB is benign, and the referral is how we make sure quickly.

items.fail: No plan to track the referral or discuss the result.
items.why: Non-specific follow-up is a common failing feedback statement.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard in a week, ring us. I’ll go through the result with you.”

timeMap.d: She minimises and asks for reassurance. Thank her for coming; don’t agree it’s nothing.
Menopause age, HRT, the bleed, discharge, other sources, parity, family history, screening.
Name the cancer fear behind the minimising and the dread of examination.
NICE NG12 referral today; what the pathway involves; most causes benign; in-person examination with control.
Chase if no contact, heavy bleeding or pain, results together. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees it is probably dryness and offers vaginal oestrogen or a watch-and-wait; no suspected cancer referral; or refers abruptly with “we need to rule out cancer” and no support; skips examination because she booked video.
wordPics.pass: Recognises PMB at 61 off HRT as an NICE NG12 suspected cancer referral; makes it today; explains most causes are benign; arranges in-person examination; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the cancer fear and the examination dread; offers choice, chaperone and control; checks screening history; explains the pathway steps; commits to reviewing the result with her; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably just dryness — let’s see if it happens again.”
avoid.instead: “Any bleeding after the menopause is something we always check, even once.”
avoid.why: Waiting for recurrence is not in line with NICE NG12.

avoid.dont: “We need to rule out cancer, so I’m sending you to the cancer clinic.”
avoid.instead: “Most bleeding like this is harmless. The urgent referral is how we make sure quickly.”
avoid.why: Blunt framing frightens a patient already minimising out of fear, and risks non-attendance.

avoid.dont: “You’ll need an internal examination — it only takes a minute.”
avoid.instead: “I heard how hard the last one was. You’re in control, with a chaperone, and we stop when you say.”
avoid.why: Brushing past the dread loses her agreement to be examined.

A bad smear years ago has left her dreading examination. A trauma-informed approach can keep her engaged.

legal.t: She has capacity and can decline referral or examination; if so, explain the risk, document the discussion and keep the door open (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Explain why, offer a chaperone, gain consent, and stop on request (GMC guidance on intimate examinations and chaperones).
Track the suspected cancer referral and make sure she is seen; tell her who will contact her and what to do if they don’t.

community.t: The Eve Appeal (gynaecological cancer charity) has information on postmenopausal bleeding and what tests involve.

redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding at 55 or over, not attributable to HRT: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Blood-stained or watery discharge, weight loss, pelvic pain
Risk factors: obesity, type 2 diabetes, nulliparity, family history
psychosocial: Mother’s “womb trouble” and fear of the same
Dread of examination after a bad smear
Living with diabetes and weight — without blame
ice: Concern: cancer, like her mother; being examined
Expectation: reassurance by video and no tests

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Bleeding after the menopause always needs checking. Most causes are harmless, but the way we make sure is an urgent referral to look at the lining of the womb.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a smoke alarm going off once. Usually it’s burnt toast, but you still check the house — quickly and properly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hoping I’d say it’s nothing because of what happened to your mum. I’d rather find out properly and fast, so you’re not lying awake guessing.”
management.psychosocial: Accommodate the examination dread with a chaperone, choice of speculum, and her control to stop.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial cancer today (NICE NG12)
Face-to-face abdominal and speculum examination with chaperone, not delaying the referral
Check cervical screening history and offer screening if due
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, pain or feeling unwell → same-day contact
Ring if no hospital contact within a week; results reviewed together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you hold a red flag against a patient who wants you to let it go. It is failed by collusion, by frightening her out of the pathway, or by skipping the examination.

items.fail: Accepting “probably dryness” and suggesting vaginal oestrogen or review if it recurs.
items.why: PMB at 61 off HRT meets the NICE NG12 referral criterion. A single episode counts.
items.fix: “Any bleeding after the menopause gets checked — I’m referring you urgently today.”

items.fail: Delaying the referral until after an examination or blood tests.
items.why: Examination matters, but the referral should not wait for it.
items.fix: Refer today and book the in-person examination alongside.

items.fail: Missing the cancer fear under “it’s nothing”.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s concerns.” Her minimising is fear, and unaddressed fear risks non-attendance.
items.fix: “You mentioned your mum — I wondered if cancer had crossed your mind?”

items.fail: Brushing past her dread of examination.
items.why: She booked video to avoid it. Without choice and control, she may not attend.
items.fix: Chaperone, smaller speculum, stop on request, talk her through each step.

items.fail: “We need to rule out cancer” with no context of how often it is benign.
items.fix: Say both truths: most PMB is benign, and the referral is how we make sure quickly.

items.fail: No plan to track the referral or discuss the result.
items.why: Non-specific follow-up is a common failing feedback statement.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard in a week, ring us. I’ll go through the result with you.”
